lesson.child_mission: Animal life cycles are sequences of stages from birth (or hatching) through growth to adult and often reproduction. Stages differ between animal groups.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Put in order: adult frog, frog eggs, tadpole. Name one stage unique to the butterfly cycle.

FEEDBACK
Eggs → tadpole → adult frog; pupa (or larva) is unique compared with the frog list.

WATCH FOR
Drawing cute animals out of order is not a life-cycle model.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Diagram three animal life cycles with labelled stages. Write one sentence comparing which stage looks most different from the adult in each.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Animal life cycles are sequences of stages from birth (or hatching) through growth to adult and often reproduction. Stages differ between animal groups.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Butterfly: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa → adult. Frog: egg → tadpole → froglet → adult. Chicken: egg → chick → adult. Order matters; skipping a stage breaks the sequence.

TRY FIRST
Put in order: adult frog, frog eggs, tadpole. Name one stage unique to the butterfly cycle.

FEEDBACK
Eggs → tadpole → adult frog; pupa (or larva) is unique compared with the frog list.
teach_steps.explain:
Animal life cycles are sequences of stages from birth (or hatching) through growth to adult and often reproduction. Stages differ between animal groups.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Drawing cute animals out of order is not a life-cycle model. Correct the claim or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
